commons:98691695.summary: In the apse of the monastery church at the foot of Mount Sinai, Christ stands in a blue mandorla of light, his white garments radiating rays toward Moses and Elijah at his sides, while Peter, James and John fall to the ground in awe. Set against an infinite gold field, it is the earliest known example of the standard Byzantine Transfiguration image and one of the finest mosaics of the age of Justinian. The setting is deeply fitting, for both Moses and Elijah met God on the mountain traditionally identified with Sinai.
facts: The monastery was founded by Emperor Justinian between 548 and 565, and the mosaic is usually dated c. 565–566, at the very end of his reign or just after his death.
A frame of medallions surrounds the scene, with the apostles above and the prophets below, joined by two contemporaries of the mosaicists: the abbot Longinus and the deacon John.

The mosaic survived Iconoclasm, Islamic rule and centuries of isolation; by the early 2000s parts around Christ's face had detached from the wall, and it was conserved between 2005 and 2010 by Rome's Centro di Conservazione Archeologica.
Saint Catherine's Monastery is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the oldest continuously inhabited Christian monasteries in the world.

commons:98691695.notes: Commons gives 'circa 600'; Wikipedia places it in Justinian's reign. In this photograph the inscriptions name Elijah at viewer's left and Moses at right, whereas Wikipedia's text says the reverse; the description follows the visible labels.

cur:manuscripts-escorial-he-cometh-with-.summary: Christ, with a red halo, sits frontally holding an open book within a great deep-blue cloud that fills the page, flanked by angels and standing figures; below, crowds of people turn and gesture in fear and mourning. The page illustrates the opening vision of the Revelation, 'Behold, he cometh with clouds'.
facts: The Escorial Beatus has 151 surviving leaves and 52 miniatures; it was probably made at San Millán de la Cogolla and was already in the Escorial library in the 16th century.
Its figures, with huge eyes and boldly patterned drapery, are among the most expressive in the Beatus tradition.
cur:manuscripts-escorial-he-cometh-with-.notes: Folio not stated on the Commons file.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-26-christ.summary: In the centre the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, bearing a torch and attended by four figures, stands in the porch of a domed church and grasps the hand of the psalmist, who approaches with a sacrificial lamb: 'one thing have I desired of the Lord ... that I may dwell in the house of the Lord'. Below, the hosts encamped against him stumble and fall. Above, a father and mother turn away from their child, 'when my father and my mother forsake me'.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-26-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-76-christ.summary: In the centre of the heavens the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, holding a scroll, walks within an elliptical mandorla among angels, and at the base of the mandorla is a wheel, a literal picture of the Latin 'in rota' — 'the voice of thy thunder was in the whirlwind'. The troubled psalmist gazes up from the left under the moon and stars, and personifications of thunder appear at the right. The drawing evokes the Lord's way through the sea.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-76-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-girona-christ-in-majest.summary: Within a great interlaced lozenge Christ sits enthroned in a round glory, holding a book and blessing, while angels fly above and the four living creatures — the symbols of the Evangelists — occupy the corners; small figures support the frame from below. The frontispiece sets the majesty of Christ at the very beginning of the commentary.
facts: The Girona Beatus was completed on 6 July 975 for an abbot Dominicus, probably at the monastery of Tábara; unusually, its painters are named: 'Ende, woman painter and servant of God', and the monk-priest Emeterius.
With 184 surviving miniatures on 284 leaves, it is one of the most richly decorated of the Beatus commentaries.
cur:manuscripts2-girona-christ-in-majest.notes: Folio 2r according to the Commons description; another Christ in Majesty in this manuscript (fol. 19r, within the Alpha) is already in the collection.

Q1748749.summary: The lid of this reliquary of the True Cross is set with nine enamel panels framed by gems and pearls. In the centre Christ sits enthroned between the Virgin and St John the Baptist, a Deesis flanked by the archangels Gabriel and Michael, while the rows above and below hold the twelve apostles. Inside lies a double-armed cross containing fragments of the True Cross, so that the lid presents Christ in glory over the relic of his Passion.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the cross inside names the emperors Constantine VII and Romanos II, who ruled jointly from 945 to 959, while the box was made later for Basil Lekapenos, probably between 963 and 985.
Compartments around the cross held ten further relics, among them the swaddling clothes and crown of thorns of Christ, belts of the Virgin and hair of John the Baptist.
It was probably brought to Germany as loot from the Fourth Crusade and is now in the Diocesan Museum at Limburg an der Lahn; the box measures 48 × 38 cm.
Q1748749.notes: Box date changed from 'c. 964–965' to Wikipedia's 'probably 963–985' (between Basil's elevation to proedros and his exile).

Q116273033.summary: Christ stands rather than hangs on the cross, his arms stretched straight and his feet planted on a patterned footrest, while two half-length angels mourn above the cross-arm. Below, the Virgin wraps herself in her mantle in grief and John, holding a book, lifts his hand toward his Lord. Made in Amalfi around 1060–70, the plaque shows the strong Byzantine influence in the ivories of southern Italy.
facts: The Met suggests that the plaque probably served as the central panel of a triptych icon.
It is about 12.9 × 8.6 cm and was given to the Met by J. Pierpont Morgan in 1917.
